text: Section 4.3 gives you the two facts this problem needs: the area under an entire PDF must equal 1, and the CDF is the running integral of the PDF [p. 125]. Write the area as one integral with \(K\) still inside it, solve for \(K\), then integrate again from \(0\) to \(b\).

label: (a)
title: Find K and sketch the PDF

name: PDF properties
text: For a continuous random variable \(X\) with PDF \(f_X(x)\): (a) \(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x\); (b) \(F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(u)\,du\); (c) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx = 1\).

title: Write the condition that the total area is 1

text: The PDF is zero outside \(0 < b \le 2\), so the integral in Theorem 4.2(c) runs only over that interval. The unknown \(K\) has to be whatever makes the area under this one hump equal to 1.

title: Evaluate the integral and solve for K

steps.why: Antiderivative of the quadratic; the lower limit contributes nothing.
Evaluate at the upper limit and set the area equal to 1 by Theorem 4.2(c).
Keep the \(K\) terms on one side; this is a single linear equation in \(K\).

text: Only the middle term of the PDF depended on \(K\), so it is no surprise that one area condition pins \(K\) down exactly. With \(K = -11/6\) the PDF is \(f_B(b) = b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1\) on \(0 < b \le 2\).

title: Check the PDF is nonnegative on (0, 2]

text: Theorem 4.2(a) demands \(f_B(b) \ge 0\), and this quadratic dips between its endpoints. The vertex of \(b^2 + Kb + 1\) sits at \(b = -K/2 = 11/12 \approx 0.917\), and that is the minimum:
At the ends of the interval, the formula gives \(f_B(0) = 1\) and \(f_B(2) = \tfrac{4}{3}\), so the curve stays positive everywhere on \((0, 2]\): a valid PDF.

title: A PDF value above 1 is fine
text: The peak value here is \(4/3 > 1\). A PDF value is not a probability, it is probability per unit length, so it can be any nonnegative number [p. 125]. What must hold is the area, not the height.

label: (a)
text: \(K = -\frac{11}{6}\). The PDF is the parabola \(f_B(b) = b^2 - \frac{11}{6}b + 1\) for \(0 < b \le 2\) and 0 otherwise: it starts at height 1, bottoms out at \(\frac{23}{144}\) near \(b = \frac{11}{12}\), and rises to \(\frac{4}{3}\) at \(b = 2\), as in the plot above.

label: (b)
title: Find and sketch the CDF of B

name: Probability Density Function (PDF)
text: The probability density function (PDF) of a continuous random variable \(X\) is \(f_X(x) = \frac{dF_X(x)}{dx}\).

title: Integrate the PDF from 0 to b

text: Since the PDF is the derivative of the CDF [p. 124], the CDF is the integral of the PDF, Theorem 4.2(b). Because \(f_B\) is zero up to \(b = 0\), the run starts at 0, and it stops at \(b = 2\), where all the probability has been used up.

title: Check the endpoints and plot points

text: A CDF must run from 0 up to 1 and never decrease (Theorem 4.1 [p. 121]). Here \(F_B(0) = 0\), and the top of the ramp lands exactly where it should:

steps.why: Substitute the top of the ramp; it equals 1 because \(K\) was chosen to make the total area 1.
Interior points to place the sketch; they increase steadily since \(f_B \ge 0\).

title: The two answers agree
text: That \(F_B(2) = 1\) is the same equation you solved in part (a), read in reverse: finding \(K\) from the area and landing at height 1 are one and the same fact. If your \(F_B(2)\) is not exactly 1, recheck \(K\).

The curve rises slowly through the middle, where the PDF bottoms out near \(b = 11/12\), and steepens toward \(b = 2\), where the PDF is tallest. Steepness of the CDF is exactly the PDF value [p. 124].

label: (b)
text: \(F_B(b) = 0\) for \(b \le 0\); \(F_B(b) = \frac{b^3}{3} - \frac{11b^2}{12} + b\) for \(0 < b \le 2\); and \(F_B(b) = 1\) for \(b > 2\), as sketched above.
